warmup.q: Two copies of the payments program, A and B, save a payment's status in a database that keeps only the write with the latest time stamp. Each copy stamps its writes with its own clock, and B's clock is 15 ms behind A's. A saves captured (the money has moved). 6 ms later, B reads captured and saves refunded. The database says OK to both. What does the next read return?
options: captured, because B's write carries the older stamp and is thrown away
An error, because the database spots that the two writes clash
warmup.why: The database keeps the write with the highest stamp, and each stamp comes from the writer's own clock. B wrote 6 ms later in real time, but its clock is 15 ms behind, so its stamp is 9 ms older than A's. The database throws B's write away and still says OK. There's no error and no clash: the order of the clocks beat the order of the events. The first option is the trap, because it trusts the stamps to match real time.

sections.h: Two clocks for two jobs: what time is it, and how long did it take?
sections.html:
The clock on your oven runs a few minutes fast. One day you set it right, and it jumps back four minutes. The kitchen timer counting down your eggs never jumps: it only counts how much time has passed. A computer has both kinds, and mixing them up has taken real systems down.

In Java and Kotlin, System.currentTimeMillis() answers "what time is it?". It returns the milliseconds since the start of 1970 in UTC, the world's reference time. That's the number you'd put in a log line or next to a payment. System.nanoTime() answers "how long did that take?". It counts nanoseconds (billionths of a second) from a starting point that nobody chose on purpose. The documentation for JDK 25, the current long-term-support version of Java, says it may only be used to measure elapsed time. On Linux, both come from clocks kept by the kernel, the core of the operating system: currentTimeMillis reads one called CLOCK_REALTIME, and nanoTime reads CLOCK_MONOTONIC. (A shortcut called the vDSO lets a program read them without a slow trip into the kernel. The Operating systems track's lesson What a kernel does: system calls and user mode explains it.)

The first kind is the time-of-day clock, or wall clock, like the oven. It tries to match real time, so it gets corrected, and a correction can be a jump. NTP, the Network Time Protocol, is how a computer asks a time server for the right time. If it finds the clock 300 ms fast, it may step it back 300 ms, and a person can set the clock by hand too. Then there are leap seconds: an extra second, added now and then to keep clocks in step with the Earth's slightly uneven spin. When one is added (the last was at the end of 2016), the day ends with 23:59:60. The Linux kernel does that by stepping its clock back one second at midnight. Subtract two wall-clock readings across a step, and the duration is wrong, perhaps negative.

That's what broke part of Cloudflare's DNS on 1 January 2017. Cloudflare runs a big network in front of many websites, and DNS is the service that turns a name like example.com into a machine's address. Its DNS program, written in the Go language, timed round trips to other servers with time.Now(), which reads the wall clock. When the leap second stepped the clock back, a round trip came out negative. The running average went negative too, and the code passed it to rand.Int63n(), which crashes the program when it's given a negative number. At the worst moment, about 0.2% of DNS questions failed. Go 1.9 later made time.Time carry a monotonic reading as well, so subtracting two times now uses it.

The monotonic clock is the kitchen timer: it never jumps. NTP may still slew it, making it tick slightly faster or slower for a while to correct its rate, but it never moves backward. Its value alone means nothing. It may count from when the machine started, and another machine, or another running JVM (the program that runs Java and Kotlin code), counts from somewhere else. So comparing nanoTime() values across machines is meaningless.

Measure durations with the timer, never with the wall clock.

So durations, timeouts and deadlines use nanoTime() or Kotlin's TimeSource.Monotonic. Points in time that must mean the same thing on another machine use the wall clock. Then you must assume it can be wrong, and the rest of this lesson is about how wrong. Linux has two more clocks you'll meet. CLOCK_BOOTTIME is monotonic, but keeps counting while the machine sleeps. CLOCK_TAI is like CLOCK_REALTIME, but counts leap seconds instead of repeating one. The Try replays Cloudflare's bug in Kotlin.

The wall clock jumps when something corrects it. Next, we'll see why it needs correcting at all.

try.title: Your clocks, and a duration that goes negative
steps: Predict: what is the smallest step of System.currentTimeMillis(), and of System.nanoTime(), on your laptop?

Run the demo. Part 1 measures both. Part 2 times a 12 ms round trip twice: once with a wall clock that is stepped back one second in the middle (as a leap second or an NTP step would do), and once with nanoTime. It passes each result to Random.nextLong(bound), which needs a positive number, as Go's rand.Int63n did.
Open WallClockDemo.kt and find the one line that would have avoided the outage.
try.expect:
currentTimeMillis: smallest step 1 ms (over 50 changes)
nanoTime:          smallest step 41 ns (over a million reads)
nanoTime now:      279138216654000 (an arbitrary origin: compare it only with this JVM's own readings)

round trip from the wall clock: -982 ms
round trip from nanoTime:       18 ms
Random.nextLong(-982) with the wall clock value: IllegalArgumentException: Random range is empty: [0, -982).
Random.nextLong(18) with the nanoTime value: 4

This run was on an Apple Silicon Mac, where nanoTime moves in steps of about 41 ns, because it reads a counter that ticks 24 million times a second. On Linux in the lab box (the course's Linux container) you'll usually see much smaller steps, and the nanoTime now value is different on every machine. The round trips vary by a few milliseconds from run to run. The wall-clock round trip is the real 18 ms minus the 1,000 ms step, and the random call throws an error, as Go's did. nanoTime doesn't see the step at all.

sections.h: Quartz drifts, NTP pulls it back, and only an error bound is honest
sections.html:
A computer's clock is a quartz crystal, a tiny piece of mineral that vibrates at a steady rate when power runs through it, plus a counter of the vibrations. Real crystals run slightly fast or slow, depending on how they were cut and on the temperature. The error is measured in parts per million (ppm): 1 ppm is 1 microsecond per second, about 86 ms a day. Google's Spanner paper assumes a worst case of 200 ppm, which is 17.28 seconds a day for a clock nobody corrects. Two machines drifting in opposite directions move apart even faster. The lab's DriftDemo runs one clock 150 ppm fast and one 120 ppm slow. It syncs them, or sets them right, at different intervals:

sync                    fast clock, max  slow clock, max   max skew between
never                          12960 ms        -10368 ms           23328 ms
every hour                       539 ms          -431 ms             970 ms
every 64 s                         9 ms            -7 ms              16 ms
every 30 s                         4 ms            -3 ms               7 ms

The gap between two machines' clocks at the same moment is called the skew. Without syncing, these two clocks are 23 seconds apart after a day. Syncing every 30 seconds keeps them within 7 ms.

NTP does the syncing. The machine asks a time server for the time and keeps four timestamps. They record when it sent the question, when the server received it, when the server replied, and when the answer arrived. From them it estimates how far off its own clock is, assuming the trip there took as long as the trip back. Often it didn't, because a queue held up one direction (Partial failure showed how common that is). Then the estimate is off by up to half the difference, and NTP can't tell. So NTP's accuracy is limited by the network: over the public internet, tens of milliseconds is typical. chrony, the NTP program on Red Hat's Linux and many others, corrects small errors by slewing and steps the clock only for large ones. Its usual setting makestep 1 3 means: step if the clock is off by more than a second in the first three updates.

Better sources shrink the error. Some network cards stamp each packet in hardware the moment it arrives, which takes the kernel's own queues out of the measurement. chrony's documentation says that with them, good switches and frequent syncs, accuracy under a microsecond on a local network may be possible. PTP, the Precision Time Protocol, is built around such hardware stamps. In November 2023, AWS, Amazon's cloud, brought this to its rented machines, called EC2. Its Time Sync Service reports a clock error bound, the most the clock may be off, of under 100 µs (microseconds) over NTP. From a PTP hardware clock on its newer machines, which AWS calls Nitro, the bound is under 40 µs, against about 1 ms before. AWS's free ClockBound program publishes that bound, so a program can read an interval, from the earliest to the latest possible time, instead of one number. The figure shows the bound's sawtooth shape between syncs.

The bound can still be wrong. Take a virtual machine, a pretend computer that shares a real one, in Google's cloud. If it's moved to another real machine while it runs, its clock can jump forward by up to 5 seconds. A machine whose NTP traffic is blocked by a firewall, a filter that stops some network traffic, drifts, and nobody notices. Leap seconds have caused outages, among them Reddit's in 2012, on Cassandra, a database that spreads data over many machines. That's why Google and AWS smear them: they slow their clocks a little over a day instead of adding the second at once. Mixing smeared and unsmeared time sources makes two clocks disagree by up to half a second. Leap seconds are on their way out. In October 2026, the CGPM, the treaty body behind the world's units of measurement, reportedly voted to stop adding them from 20 May 2027. That rests on news reports and secondary summaries; the course hasn't seen the official text, and the second edition of Designing Data-Intensive Applications still says 2035.

One more fact shapes how you test all this. A container is a program that the kernel keeps apart from others, with its own view of files and processes. (The Operating systems track's lesson Containers are processes: namespaces and cgroups explains them.) Containers on one machine share the kernel's wall clock. Linux time namespaces can shift the monotonic and boot clocks for one container, but never CLOCK_REALTIME. The Try proves it. To give one copy of a program a skewed clock, you hand its code a different java.time.Clock, an object the code asks for the time. That's what the lab does.

So every clock is a little wrong, and an honest one says by how much. Next, we'll see what happens to data when two wrong clocks disagree.

try.title: Containers share one wall clock
steps: Start Docker, the program that runs containers. From the labs folder, run the commands below. The first two start two different containers and print the kernel's boot id, a random id the kernel picks each time the machine starts.
The third tries to set the wall clock inside an ordinary container. Predict whether it works.

The fourth runs in the privileged box, a container allowed to do more. It prints the uptime (which comes from CLOCK_BOOTTIME) and the wall clock. Then it does the same inside a new time namespace whose boot and monotonic clocks are moved forward one day. Which number moves?

code.title: from the labs folder
code.html: docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm -T box cat /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm -T box-priv cat /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm -T box date -s '2026-01-01' docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm -T box-priv bash -c 'cut -d" " -f1 /proc/uptime; date -u +%T; unshare -T --boottime=86400 --monotonic=86400 bash -c "cut -d\" \" -f1 /proc/uptime; date -u +%T"'

date: cannot set date: Operation not permitted

Both containers print the same boot id: one kernel, so one CLOCK_REALTIME. date -s understands the date and is refused, because an ordinary container lacks the permission to set the clock; even a privileged one could only set it for every container on the machine at once. sections.h: Last write wins throws away the write that came second
sections.html:
Remember the tills: the owner kept only the latest receipt for each item. Many databases do the same with two writes to one item. They keep the write with the highest timestamp and drop the other, a rule called last write wins, or LWW. The Replication track's lesson Concurrent writes: last write wins, version vectors and CRDTs met it. This lesson asks where the timestamps come from. Cassandra and ScyllaDB, two databases that spread data over many machines, take them from the client, the program that sends the write. Cassandra's Java driver, the library a Java program uses to talk to it, stamps each write with the client machine's clock, in microseconds. That way a database machine never has to ask anyone what time it is.

Here is what that does to a payment, step by step in the stepper. Two copies of the payments program write one payment's status. The lab calls them pod-a and pod-b, after the name one popular tool uses for a running copy of a program. The status moves through four values: captured (the money has moved), refunded (given back to the customer), settled (paid out to the shop) and chargeback (the customer's bank took it back after a complaint).

pod-a writes captured, stamped 10:00:00.002 by its clock. pod-b, whose clock is 15 ms behind, reads captured 6 ms later and writes refunded. pod-b's stamp says 09:59:59.993, so the database keeps captured, drops refunded, and says OK to both. Nothing logs an error. The refund was confirmed, and it's gone. And pod-b keeps losing: every pod-b write that follows a pod-a write is dropped, until pod-b's clock passes the highest stamp pod-a wrote.

The skew doesn't need to be large. It only has to be larger than the gap between two causally related writes, where the second was decided after its writer saw the first. In the lab the gap is 6 ms. A skew of 6 ms loses nothing, and 7 ms loses every write from the slow copy that follows one from the fast copy. Now add 0 to 50 ms of thinking time between writes. A 10 ms skew loses 4% of confirmed writes, 20 ms loses 14%, and 100 ms or more loses half: every write the slow copy makes. Over the public internet, NTP errors of 10 to 20 ms are ordinary.

Kyle Kingsbury measured this in Cassandra in 2013, in one of his Jepsen tests, which put databases through faults and count what they lose. His test programs updated one value at QUORUM, a Cassandra setting that waits until most copies of the data have the write. They wrote one at a time, behind a perfect outside lock that let only one program write at once. Cassandra still lost 285 of 1,009 confirmed writes, about 28%. The timestamps, not the lock's order, decided which write survived.

Never let two machines' clocks decide which write wins.

Better NTP shrinks the window; it doesn't close it. The fixes stop comparing timestamps from different machines. Write rows that never change, under unique keys (one row per status change, keyed by a random unique id called a UUID), and read them all. Use types that merge, such as Cassandra's sets and counters. Use a conditional write, one that applies only if the current value is what you expect: the lightweight transaction from the Transactions track's lesson Transactions in NoSQL. Or make the order explicit. Version vectors, counters that each copy keeps, do that (the Replication track). So does a logical clock, a counter that orders events without reading any clock (lesson 6 of this track). When you do need real time, the next section shows how to get it safely.

try.title: How much skew loses how much
steps: Predict: two copies take turns updating one status, each reading it first, with 0 to 50 ms of thinking time between writes. What share of confirmed writes is lost with 20 ms of skew? With 1 second?
Run the demo. It prints the stepper's trace, then 1,000 writes for each skew.
Why does the loss stop growing at 50%? Rerun the trace part with -Pargs='5'.
try.expect:
pod-b's clock is 15 ms behind. Each write follows a read of the one before it.
round  writer  value       true time      stamp          after the OK, a read returns
1      pod-a   captured    10:00:00.002   10:00:00.002   captured
2      pod-b   refunded    10:00:00.008   09:59:59.993   captured   <- lost
3      pod-a   settled     10:00:00.014   10:00:00.014   settled
4      pod-b   chargeback  10:00:00.020   10:00:00.005   settled   <- lost

1,000 writes alternating between the pods, 0 to 50 ms of think time between them
pod-b behind   acknowledged     lost
0 ms                   1000     0.0%
5 ms                   1000     0.0%
10 ms                  1000     4.2%
20 ms                  1000    13.8%
50 ms                  1000    42.8%
100 ms                 1000    50.0%
1000 ms                1000    50.0%

acknowledged counts the writes the store said OK to: every one of them. Losses start once the skew is larger than some of the gaps between a fast-copy write and the next slow-copy write (6 ms plus thinking time). They stop at 50%, because once the skew is larger than every gap, each slow-copy write is lost and each fast-copy write survives. With -Pargs='5' the trace loses nothing: 5 ms is less than the 6 ms gap.

sections.h: Clocks that admit their error: TrueTime, ClockBound and commit wait
sections.html:
The fixes above give up on ordering by real time. Sometimes you need it. Say one transaction, a group of changes a database makes all together or not at all, finishes. Then another starts, on a machine far away that never talked to the first. The second must see the first one's changes. Spanner, Google's database that spans datacenters around the world, gets that from a clock that admits its error.

The clock is called TrueTime, and its now() doesn't return a time. It returns an interval, from earliest to latest, that contains the true time as long as the clock hardware stays within its assumptions. Google keeps the interval small with GPS receivers and atomic clocks in every datacenter. The 2012 Spanner paper gives its half-width, called ε (epsilon): the most the clock may be off in either direction. It's a sawtooth from about 1 to 7 ms over each 30-second sync, and 4 ms most of the time. That assumes 200 ppm of drift, and it's the shape in the second section's figure.

Spanner's commit, the moment a transaction's changes become final, uses the interval twice. First it stamps the transaction with a time no earlier than latest, so the stamp is not yet in the past on any honest clock. Then, before it lets anyone see the commit, it waits until earliest has passed the stamp. Now the stamp is in the past on every honest clock. This is commit wait, and it lasts about 2ε. Any transaction that starts after that moment, on any machine, reads a latest later than the stamp and gets a larger one. Timestamp order now matches real-time order, with no message between the two machines. The lab builds exactly this, and the Try shows the price: the wait is about twice the bound.

The shop's tills could follow the same rule. Each till knows it may be up to 15 seconds off. It prints the latest time it could be, and holds the receipt for 30 seconds before it hands it over. Then any receipt printed later, at any till, carries a later time. The picture breaks on the numbers and on who watches. Tills are off by seconds, and a clerk would notice. Machines are off by milliseconds, write thousands of times a second, and no person ever reads the stamps.

So ε is the number that matters. With TrueTime's 2012 figures, commit wait costs several milliseconds per commit. With AWS's 2023 bounds under 40 µs, it would be under 100 µs, and ClockBound hands the interval to any program. YugabyteDB, a database that spreads over many machines, can use ClockBound as its time source on AWS. CockroachDB, another such database, takes a different road and doesn't wait on every commit. It assumes a maximum offset between machines' clocks. That's 500 ms by default, and 250 ms is recommended for new clusters (groups of machines working as one) spread across parts of the world. A read may find a value stamped a little after its own read time, within that offset. It can't tell whether the value was written before it started, so it starts again at a later time.

Both designs are only as good as the bound, and both check it. A CockroachDB machine shuts itself down when its clock is out of step with at least half of the other machines by 80% of the maximum offset. YugabyteDB machines stop when the skew passes their own 500 ms limit. The lab's last test shows why: a copy that is 20 ms behind, but believes its bound is 5 ms, loses writes even with commit wait.

A clock bound is a promise. Check it, and stop when it breaks.

The Consistency and consensus track's lesson Distributed SQL: Spanner, CockroachDB and Aurora DSQL builds on this, and lesson 6 of this track orders events with no physical clock at all. Every design here also assumes that a program notices time passing while it works, and that isn't always true.

try.title: The price of commit wait
steps: The same chain of writes as before, but each copy stamps with latest and waits until earliest passes the stamp. Both copies sync every second. Predict pod-b's average wait when its clock is 20 ms behind and its bound is an honest 20 ms.
Run the demo. The last row lies: pod-b is 20 ms behind, but claims a 5 ms bound.
Why does pod-a wait 3 ms, even though its clock is exact?
try.expect:
pod-b's clock                          lost  pod-a waits (avg)  pod-b waits (avg)
1 ms behind, bound 1 ms                   0             3.0 ms             3.0 ms
4 ms behind, bound 4 ms                   0             3.0 ms             9.0 ms
7 ms behind, bound 7 ms                   0             3.0 ms            15.0 ms
20 ms behind, bound 20 ms                 0             3.0 ms            41.0 ms
250 ms behind, bound 250 ms               0             3.0 ms           501.0 ms
20 ms behind, bound claims 5 ms          71             3.0 ms            11.0 ms

With honest bounds nothing is lost, even 250 ms behind, and the price is the wait: about twice the bound. (Each bound is the stated one plus about 1 ms of assumed drift since the last sync, and the wait starts after the store's 2 ms round trip.) pod-a's clock is exact, but it can't know that, so it waits out its own 1 ms bound plus drift too. With a bound that lies, commit wait is too short, and 71 of 1,000 confirmed writes are lost.

opening:
Picture a shop with two tills. Each one prints the time on every receipt, and till B runs 15 seconds slow. A customer buys a jacket at till A and returns it at till B ten seconds later. That evening the owner keeps only the latest receipt for each item. By the printed times, the return came 5 seconds before the sale, so she keeps the sale. The books now say the jacket was never returned.

It's tempting to trust printed times. Computers set their clocks from the internet, and your phone always seems right. But "right" means within a few milliseconds, sometimes far more, and computers do things a few milliseconds apart.

Detecting failure: timeouts, heartbeats and gray failure ended on a question: how far can a machine trust its own clock? In this lesson, we'll meet the two clocks every computer has and measure how far they drift. Then we'll lose real data to a slow clock, and see how one database waits out its clock's error. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with two tills that disagreed by 15 seconds, and a return that vanished when only the latest receipt was kept. Computers have the same problem in milliseconds. Wall clocks jump and drift, a store that trusts them drops writes while saying OK, and real-time order needs a clock that admits its error.

On a Mac, run sntp time.apple.com in a terminal. It prints how far your clock is from Apple's time server, and an error bound. One run gave +0.006557 +/- 0.015556: about 7 ms off, give or take 16. On Linux, chronyc tracking shows the same.

Next, we'll freeze a program in the middle of its work, and see why even a perfect clock can't warn it that it acted too late.

compare.title: Timing an issuer call

a.label: Wall clock: wrong across a step
a.title: IssuerTimer.kt
a.html: val start = System.currentTimeMillis() val code = issuer.authorize(key, amount) val tookMs = System.currentTimeMillis() - start // an NTP step in between: wrong, maybe negative latency.record(tookMs)

b.label: Monotonic clock: always a duration
b.title: IssuerTimer.kt
b.html: val mark = TimeSource.Monotonic.markNow() // reads System.nanoTime() on the JVM val code = issuer.authorize(key, amount) val took = mark.elapsedNow() // a Duration, never negative latency.record(took.inWholeMilliseconds)

compare.note: Both read a clock twice and subtract. The left one reads CLOCK_REALTIME, which NTP, a person or a leap second can move either way between the two reads. The right one reads CLOCK_MONOTONIC through Kotlin's TimeSource.Monotonic, which only ever moves forward, so elapsedNow() is a real duration. The wall clock's number is still the right thing to log next to the result, as the moment the call happened.

worked.title: Commit wait, built from a clock that admits its error

steps.say: Model a machine's clock in virtual time, a pretend clock that the simulation moves forward itself. The reading is the true time, plus the offset the clock had at its last sync, plus the drift since. The machine can read this number, but not the offset inside it.
steps.code: override fun millis(): Long { val elapsed = sim.now - syncedAt return sim.now + offsetAtSync + elapsed * driftPpm / 1_000_000 }

steps.say: What the machine does know is a bound: how far off it was allowed to be at the sync, plus the worst drift it assumes since. Round up, because a bound must never be too small.
steps.code: fun errorBoundMs(): Long { val elapsed = sim.now - syncedAt return boundAtSync + Math.ceilDiv(elapsed * maxDriftPpm, 1_000_000L) // 1 ms + 6 ms after 30 s at 200 ppm }

steps.say: Report the reading the way TrueTime and ClockBound do: as an interval that holds the true time, if the bound is honest.
steps.code: fun bounds(): TimeInterval = millis().let { now -> val e = errorBoundMs() TimeInterval(now - e, now + e) }

steps.say: Stamp a write with latest. The true time can't be later than that yet, so no write that already happened anywhere can carry a larger stamp from an honest clock.
steps.code: val stamp = clock.bounds().latest store.write(Write(value, stamp, name)) { /* acknowledged */ }

steps.say: Wait until earliest passes the stamp before telling anyone the write is done. From then on every honest clock reads later than the stamp, so every write that depends on this one gets a larger stamp. The wait is about 2ε.
steps.code: fun check() { if (clock.bounds().earliest > stamp) done(sim.now - ackedAt) // the stamp is in everyone's past else sim.after(1) { check() } }

lab.title: Drifting clocks, a register that loses writes, and commit wait
steps: Read the given parts. Sim keeps the true time, starting at 10:00:00 UTC on 7 November 2026. DriftingClock is a java.time.Clock, so code can take it wherever it would take Clock.systemUTC(). causalChain in Registers.kt runs writers that each read the register before they write. Run the tests from the labs folder: all 16 fail.

Exercise 1: DriftingClock.millis, errorBoundMs and bounds. Run --tests 'sfz.dist.l03.ClockTest': 8 pass. They include 17.28 s a day at 200 ppm, the 1-to-7 ms sawtooth, a sync that moves the clock backward, and a jqwik property (jqwik runs one check with many random inputs) that an honest interval always contains the true time.
Exercise 2: LwwRegister.apply. The tests with plain writes now pass, among them a writer whose clock is 20 ms behind loses every write that follows the other's: 100 OKs, and 50 writes gone.

Exercise 3: Writer.writeWithCommitWait. Run all 16. The property test tries 200 random offsets, bounds, thinking times and seeds, and finds no lost write; commit wait is only as good as the bound finds some.
hints: millis: sim.now + offsetAtSync + (sim.now - syncedAt) * driftPpm / 1_000_000. It's whole-number division, so 0.5 ms of drift reads as 0.
errorBoundMs: Math.ceilDiv(a, b) rounds a positive division up (JDK 18 and later, and the labs compile for 21).
LWW tie-break: write.timestampMs == c.timestampMs && write.writer > c.writer. You can compare strings with >, because Kotlin turns it into compareTo.
In writeWithCommitWait, read clock.bounds().latest once, before sending. Inside the store's OK, define a local fun check() that calls done, or schedules itself again with sim.after(1) { check() }.

drill.title: Commit wait from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write writeWithCommitWait(value, done) given clock.bounds(), store.write(write, ack) and sim.after(ms, action). Then answer in one comment each: why is the stamp latest and not the plain reading, and why does the wait end when earliest passes the stamp?

answer.html: fun writeWithCommitWait(value: String, done: (waitedMs: Long) -> Unit) { val stamp = clock.bounds().latest store.write(Write(value, stamp, name)) { val ackedAt = sim.now fun check() { if (clock.bounds().earliest > stamp) done(sim.now - ackedAt) else sim.after(1) { check() } } check() } } // latest: the true time is at most latest, so this stamp is not below any write that already happened // (each of those was stamped at or below the true time when it was made, and waited until its stamp passed). // earliest > stamp: the true time is now past the stamp, so any write that starts after done() is // stamped with a latest that is past it too. Real-time order and stamp order agree.

recap: The wall clock (currentTimeMillis, CLOCK_REALTIME) gives points in time and can jump either way. The monotonic clock (nanoTime, CLOCK_MONOTONIC) gives durations and means nothing across machines.
Quartz drifts up to about 200 ppm, 17 seconds a day. NTP over the internet keeps clocks within tens of milliseconds, and hardware stamps and PTP bring cloud bounds under 100 µs (AWS: under 40 µs).
Containers on one machine share its wall clock, and time namespaces shift only the monotonic and boot clocks, so tests give code a skewed clock through java.time.Clock.

Last write wins with stamps from each writer's clock silently drops a write that depended on an earlier one, whenever its writer's clock lags by more than the gap between them. Jepsen lost 28% of confirmed Cassandra writes.

A clock that reports [earliest, latest] lets Spanner wait about 2ε so that stamp order matches real-time order. CockroachDB instead assumes a maximum offset (500 ms) and restarts reads it can't order.
The limit: every such design is only as good as its bound, so machines that drift past it shut themselves down. Ordering events without trusting any clock needs another tool, which lesson 6 builds.

explain.prompt: A friend's team wants to sort payment events from three programs, on three machines, by the time each program stamps on them, "since every machine syncs its clock". Explain what can go wrong, with numbers, and what you'd do instead.
explain.answer: Syncing keeps each machine near UTC, but not exactly. Over a normal network the error is milliseconds to tens of milliseconds, a step can move a clock by hundreds of milliseconds, and a virtual machine that is moved can jump by seconds. So two machines' clocks can disagree by more than the time between two related events. Say the refund program writes a refund 6 ms after the payment program wrote the capture, and the refund machine's clock is 15 ms behind. Then the refund gets the earlier stamp. Sorting by time puts it before the capture, and a last-write-wins store keeps the capture and silently drops the refund, while saying OK to both. Better syncing only shrinks that window. Instead, I'd avoid comparing clocks from different machines. I'd give each payment one place that orders its events (a counter in the database, or a version number checked with a conditional write), or keep the events as rows that never change and merge them, or carry a logical clock. If we truly need real-time order across machines, we need a clock that reports its error, like ClockBound, and we must wait out that error before saying a write is done, which is what Spanner does.

deeper.html:
How NTP estimates the offset. Call t1 the client's send time, t2 the server's receive time, t3 the server's send time and t4 the client's receive time. The offset estimate is ((t2 − t1) + (t3 − t4)) / 2, and the round trip is (t4 − t1) − (t3 − t2). The estimate is exact only if both directions took the same time; any difference ends up, halved, in the offset. chrony and ntpd combine many samples from several servers and throw away outliers. Both report a root dispersion (how much error has built up along the chain of time servers) and a root delay (the round trip to the top of that chain). That's where ClockBound's bound starts: the absolute offset, plus the root dispersion, plus half the root delay.

Leap smearing. Google's public NTP servers spread a leap second over 24 hours, noon to noon UTC, by slowing their clocks by about 11.6 ppm, well inside what NTP clients can follow. AWS's NTP service is smeared too, while its PTP hardware clock is not, so AWS advises against mixing the two sources on one machine. With leap seconds reportedly ending in 2027, smearing becomes history. The bigger fear had been the first negative leap second ever, a day one second short, which almost no software has been tested against.

Hybrid logical clocks keep a 64-bit timestamp close to physical time, while making sure a message's receiver always stamps later than its sender, whatever the clocks say. CockroachDB and YugabyteDB use them alongside their offset limits. Lesson 6 builds one.

Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 9, covers clocks and the trouble with relying on them in the same order. Note that its leap-second date comes from before the reported 2026 decision.
